title: Draft Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of inter-State Transmission Charges and Losses) (Fifth Amendment) Regulations, 2026
summary: CERC proposes a further change to its draft Fifth Amendment of the Sharing Regulations (first published on 31.07.2026). The supplementary draft would add a new waiver of inter-State transmission charges for wind, solar and wind-solar hybrid projects that have a PPA or PSA of at least seven years with a drawee DIC signed on or before 31.03.2027, but whose commissioning is held up because the transmission system is not ready. If such a project achieves COD within two months of its GNA becoming effective, it would get a waiver tied to the later of its connectivity start date and SCOD, for up to the contract tenure and at most 25 years from COD. Projects qualifying under both the existing trajectory and this route would have to choose one, within 30 days of COD, and the choice would be binding. This is a proposal; comments are invited until 27 November 2026.
proposes: New Regulation 13(2)(h-i): ISTS waiver for wind, solar and wind-solar hybrid projects delayed by non-availability of transmission
Eligibility: PPA or PSA of at least 7 years with a drawee DIC (directly, via a trader or REIA) signed on or before 31.03.2027
Project must achieve COD within two months of its GNA becoming effective
PPA and PSA copies to be filed with CTUIL and NLDC by 30.04.2027
Waiver lapses if the contract is terminated early or COD is missed; the Table 1 trajectory then applies
New Regulation 13(2)(h-ii): one-time binding choice between the existing waiver and the new route, within 30 days of COD
Projects already commissioned may opt in within one month of the amendment taking effect
amends: CERC (Sharing of Inter-State Transmission Charges and Losses) Regulations, 2020

impact.headline: Renewable project delayed by transmission? A proposed ISTS charge waiver depends on a contract signed by 31.03.2027.
checks: Is your delay due to non-availability of the transmission system, beyond your connectivity start date or SCOD?
Do you have, or can you sign, a PPA or PSA of at least seven years with a drawee DIC by 31.03.2027?
Can you reach COD within two months of your GNA becoming effective?
Is your contract direct, or through a trader or REIA (both legs must then be signed and filed)?
impact.market_note: If adopted, wind, solar and wind-solar projects whose COD slipped because ISTS was not ready keep the transmission-charge waiver for the whole contract term, up to 25 years from COD. Eligibility turns on a contract: a PPA or PSA of at least seven years with a drawee DIC, signed by 31.03.2027.

key_points.text: Eligible: wind, solar or wind-solar hybrid projects delayed by non-availability of transmission beyond the later of the connectivity start date or SCOD, that reach COD within two months of their GNA becoming effective
The draft table ties the waiver to the later of those dates (cut-off 30.06.2025, with steps to 30.06.2028) and allows it for the contract tenure, capped at 25 years from COD
The waiver falls back to the Table 1 trajectory if COD is not reached within two months of GNA, or if the filed PPA or PSA is terminated early
One-time, binding choice between the existing waiver under sub-clause (a) and the new route, declared within 30 days of COD
Projects already commissioned can opt in within one month of the amendment; the waiver then runs from the day power is scheduled under the eligible contract

procurement.text: Sign a PPA or PSA of at least 7 years with a drawee DIC, directly or through a trader or REIA, on or before 31.03.2027
Through a trader or REIA: both legs (PPA with the generator, PSA with the drawee DIC) must be signed by 31.03.2027 and filed
File copies of the PPA and PSA with CTUIL and NLDC by 30.04.2027; contracts signed later or filed late are not eligible
Extensions of a filed contract keep the waiver, up to 25 years from COD

discoms.comment: If adopted, drawee DICs buying under eligible contracts would see ISTS charges waived on that drawal for the contract tenure, which favours signing such contracts before 31.03.2027.

re_developers.comment: If adopted, a project stranded by late transmission keeps ISTS charge waiver for its contract term (up to 25 years from COD), but only with a 7-year-plus PPA or PSA signed by 31.03.2027 and COD within two months of GNA.

transmission.comment: If adopted, CTUIL and NLDC hold the record: PPA and PSA copies by 30.04.2027 and each project's binding undertaking within 30 days of COD.

traders.comment: If adopted, trader- and REIA-intermediated contracts qualify, provided both the PPA and the PSA are signed by 31.03.2027 and filed with CTUIL and NLDC.

open_questions: This supplementary draft does not say how the waived charges are recovered from other ISTS users; check the main draft of 31.07.2026.
The waiver table in the PDF is laid out as a grid that extracts poorly; confirm each date step against the PDF before relying on it.
Comments are due 27.11.2026 (from CERC's listing, not this notice).

discoms.position: As a drawee DIC we support certainty on transmission charges for renewable power contracted before 31.03.2027. We ask the Commission to state who bears the charges that are waived, and to protect the buyer where a waiver ends through no act of the buyer.

points.clause: Sub-clause (h-i): waiver for the tenure of the contract
points.comment: The draft grants a waiver for the contract tenure, up to 25 years from COD, but does not say how the waived charges are recovered. If they are spread over other DICs, our charges for the rest of our drawal rise. [Add your GNA and current monthly ISTS charges.]
points.suggestion: State the recovery mechanism in the Regulations and publish an estimate of the waived amount and its effect on other DICs.

points.clause: Proviso (i) and (ii): filing of PPA and PSA with CTUIL and NLDC by 30.04.2027
points.comment: Eligibility turns on documents filed by the generator or intermediary. The drawee DIC has no way to confirm that its contract has been accepted as eligible before bills are raised.
points.suggestion: Require CTUIL to publish the list of contracts accepted under sub-clause (h-i), with the drawee DIC named, by [31.05.2027].

points.clause: Proviso (v) and (vi): waiver ceases on early termination or late COD
points.comment: If the generator misses the two-month COD window, charges revert to the Table 1 trajectory. The buyer contracted on the basis of a waiver and would bear charges caused by the generator's delay.
points.suggestion: Provide that charges arising because the generator fails a condition of sub-clause (h-i) are payable by the generator, unless the contract says otherwise.

points.clause: Proviso (iii): extension of a filed PPA or PSA
points.comment: We support the waiver continuing when a filed contract is extended, up to 25 years from COD.
points.suggestion: Confirm that an extension on revised commercial terms between the same parties also qualifies.

discoms.closing: We request the Commission to consider these comments and to grant us an opportunity to be heard before the Regulations are finalised.

re_developers.position: We support the proposed sub-clauses (h-i) and (h-ii): a project that is ready but cannot commission because the transmission system is late should not lose the waiver it was bid on. Our comments are on the conditions, which as drafted could exclude projects that are delayed for exactly the reason the amendment addresses.

points.clause: Sub-clause (h-i): PPA or PSA to be signed on or before 31.03.2027
points.comment: Eligibility depends on a contract of at least seven years being signed by 31.03.2027, and a contract signed later is not eligible. Where the generator has an award but the buyer-side PSA is still to be signed by the intermediary, the date is outside the generator's control. [Add your project's award date and PSA status.]
points.suggestion: Treat a project as eligible if either the PPA or the PSA is signed by 31.03.2027 and the other is signed within a further [six] months.

points.clause: Sub-clause (h-i): COD within two months of the GNA becoming effective
points.comment: Two months from GNA effectiveness is short for a project that could not complete commissioning tests until the transmission system was available, and a project that misses it falls back to the Table 1 trajectory for its whole capacity.
points.suggestion: Allow [six] months, and apply the waiver to the capacity that achieves COD within the window where a project is commissioned in parts.

points.clause: Proviso (v) and (vi): waiver ceases if the PPA or PSA is terminated early
points.comment: The waiver ends on early termination whatever the cause. A generator would lose it even where the buyer defaults, which also weakens the generator's position in any payment dispute.
points.suggestion: Keep the waiver where the contract is terminated for the buyer's default and a replacement contract of at least seven years is filed within [six] months.

points.clause: Sub-clause (h-ii): binding option within thirty days of COD
points.comment: The choice between sub-clause (a) and sub-clause (h-i) is permanent and must be made within thirty days of COD, when the first months of scheduling data are not yet available.
points.suggestion: Allow ninety days, and confirm that the option can be exercised separately for each part of the capacity, as the words 'corresponding capacity' suggest.

points.clause: Table 6: waiver period and percentages
points.comment: The table that sets the waiver against the later of the two dates is difficult to read in the published draft, and the percentages cannot be matched to the date ranges with confidence.
points.suggestion: Publish Table 6 in a clear row and column form with a worked example before the Regulations are notified.

re_developers.closing: We request the Commission to consider these comments and to grant us an opportunity to be heard before the Regulations are finalised.

traders.position: We welcome the express inclusion of contracts through a trading licensee or Renewable Energy Implementing Agency. Our comments concern the back-to-back signing condition, which is harder to meet for intermediated contracts than for direct ones.

points.clause: Proviso (ii): both PPA and PSA to be signed on or before 31.03.2027
points.comment: For an intermediated sale both legs must be signed by the cut-off and filed. The two legs are rarely signed on the same day, and the buyer-side approval often comes later. [Add the capacity you hold awaiting PSA.]
points.suggestion: Treat the contract as eligible where one leg is signed by 31.03.2027 and the other within [six] months, with filing within thirty days of the second signature.

points.clause: Sub-clause (h-i)(a): start date of connectivity 'as on the date of signing of PPA or PSA'
points.comment: For intermediated contracts the draft refers to the date of the PSA. Where the PPA and PSA are signed on different dates, the connectivity start date communicated by CTUIL may have changed in between.
points.suggestion: Clarify that the date of the earlier of the two contracts governs.

points.clause: Proviso (iv): a new PPA or PSA after the cut-off is not eligible
points.comment: If a drawee DIC defaults and the PSA is terminated, the intermediary cannot re-tie the same capacity to another buyer without the project losing its waiver.
points.suggestion: Allow substitution of the drawee DIC for the unexpired tenure where the replacement PSA is filed within [six] months of termination.

traders.closing: We request the Commission to consider these comments and to grant us an opportunity to be heard before the Regulations are finalised.

title: DRAFT TNERC (Deviation settlement mechanism and related matters) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes new Deviation Settlement Mechanism Regulations that would replace its 2019 regulations for generators (other than wind, solar and hybrid) and buyers connected to the intra-State transmission or distribution system. The draft adopts a market-linked DSM framework, in which deviation charges are linked to power exchange prices, and sets state-specific frequency discipline provisions to keep entities to their schedules in the interest of grid security. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: Replaces the TNERC DSM Regulations, 2019
Applies to generators other than wind, solar and hybrid, and to buyers on the intra-State system
Market-linked DSM framework, with deviation charges referenced to power exchange prices (ACP)
State-specific frequency discipline provisions
amends: Replaces TNERC (Deviation Settlement Mechanism and Related Matters) Regulations, 2019

title: Draft TNERC (Battery Energy Storage Systems) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes a complete framework for battery energy storage in Tamil Nadu. The draft classifies BESS as standalone, co-located with renewable or conventional plants, embedded, behind-the-meter, hybrid RE-BESS and multi-location systems, and recognises captive, utility-owned, third-party, merchant and hybrid ownership models. It sets planning and installation rules, including a minimum project size and grid-forming power conversion requirements, procurement routes (Section 63 bidding, Section 62 tariffs, self-owned EPC, central or state agencies and developer-led procurement), a two-part tariff of storage capacity charge and storage energy charge, normative cost parameters, tariffs for BESS co-located with solar, wind and conventional plants, third-party settlement, and technical and safety standards. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: BESS classes: standalone, co-located, embedded, behind-the-meter, hybrid RE-BESS, multi-location
Ownership models: captive, utility-owned, third-party, merchant, hybrid
Minimum project size and grid-forming (GFM) PCS requirement
Procurement: Section 63 bidding, Section 62, EPC, central/state agencies, developer-led procurement
Two-part tariff: storage capacity charge and storage energy charge rate
Tariff rules for BESS co-located with solar, wind and conventional generators
Third-party commercial agreements, settlement timelines and technical standards

title: Draft TNERC (Determination of State Load Despatch Centre Fees and Charges) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes regulations to determine the fees and charges of the State Load Despatch Centre under a multi-year tariff framework. The draft sets a business plan and capital expenditure plan for SLDC, separate accounts, the components of SLDC's annual revenue requirement (capital cost, debt-equity, return on equity, interest, depreciation, O&M, working capital, RLDC fees, SRPC charges and BESS-related expenditure, non-tariff income), registration with SLDC, the determination of system operation charges and scheduling charges, billing, late payment surcharge and default, and the public consultation process for SLDC tariff petitions, with a transition for true-up of FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: MYT framework for SLDC with business plan and capital expenditure plan
SLDC ARR components, including RLDC fees, SRPC charges and BESS-related expenditure
Registration with SLDC
System operation charges and scheduling charges
Billing, late payment surcharge and default
True-up of FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27 as a transitional provision

title: Draft TNERC Forecasting, Scheduling and Deviation Settlement and Related Matters for Wind, Solar and Hybrid Generations (with or without ESS) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes to revise its forecasting, scheduling and deviation settlement framework for wind and solar generators and extend it to wind-solar hybrid projects, with or without energy storage. The draft covers the forecasting and scheduling code, treatment of gaming, appointment of Qualified Coordinating Agencies (QCAs), deviation settlement for intra-State and inter-State transactions, metering, deviation accounting, payment security, de-pooling of deviation charges and intimation of curtailment. TNERC notes that it is acting suo motu, partly on prayers made in M.P. No. 57 of 2025, including stronger penalties for not appointing a QCA. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: Extends the framework to wind-solar hybrid projects, with or without ESS
Forecasting and scheduling code, with provisions against gaming
Principles for appointing QCAs; stronger consequences for not appointing one
Deviation settlement for intra-State and inter-State transactions
Metering, deviation accounting, payment security and de-pooling of charges
Intimation of curtailment and energy accounting
amends: TNERC (Forecasting, Scheduling and Deviation Settlement and Related Matters for Wind and Solar Generation) Regulations, 2024

title: Draft TNERC (Multi Year Tariff for Distribution) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes new Multi Year Tariff Regulations for distribution licensees in Tamil Nadu, setting how the distribution company's annual revenue requirement and retail tariffs will be determined for the next control period. The draft covers the MYT petition and mid-term review, controllable and uncontrollable factors and how gains and losses are shared, power procurement planning and a Fuel and Power Purchase Adjustment Surcharge (FPPAS), financial principles (capital cost, debt-equity, depreciation, return on equity, interest), components of ARR including sales forecast, distribution losses and O&M expenses, and the cross-subsidy surcharge and additional surcharge that open access consumers pay. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: MYT framework, petitions, mid-term review and true-up for distribution licensees
Controllable and uncontrollable factors, with pass-through of gains and losses
Power procurement plan, additional procurement, treatment of surplus power
Fuel and Power Purchase Adjustment Surcharge (FPPAS)
Financial norms: capital cost, debt-equity, depreciation, RoE, interest on loans and working capital
ARR components: sales forecast, distribution losses, capital investment plan, O&M, bad debts, non-tariff income
Cross-subsidy surcharge and additional surcharge for open access consumers
amends: Replaces the TNERC multi-year tariff framework for distribution licensees

title: Draft TNERC(Recovery of Expenses and Charges by Licensees and System Operator) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes regulations on the expenses, charges and fees that distribution licensees, transmission licensees and the SLDC may recover from applicants and users. For distribution, the draft covers the scope of charges for new connections, execution of works by applicants, estimates and adjustment, withdrawal of applications, restoration after permanent disconnection and charges for prosumers. For transmission, it covers deposit contribution works, connectivity and evacuation infrastructure, system study and processing charges and withdrawal of connectivity applications. It also sets SLDC system operation, study and registration charges, provisions for open access users, an aggregation framework with common evacuation, a schedule of charges, and transparency and grievance provisions. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: Distribution: charges for new connections, applicant-executed works, estimates, restoration of supply, prosumer charges
Transmission: deposit works, connectivity and evacuation infrastructure, system study and processing charges
SLDC: system operation, studies, communication and grid support, registration charges
Provisions for open access users and an aggregation framework with common evacuation
Enabling provision for a policy facilitation fee by a government-designated agency
Schedule of charges, transparency and grievance redressal

title: Draft TNERC (Terms and Conditions for Determination of Conventional Generation Tariff) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes new tariff regulations for conventional generating stations (thermal and hydro, including pumped hydro storage). The draft covers applications for tariff and in-principle approval, the true-up methodology for FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27, capital investment plans and capital cost, IDC and IEDC, sale of infirm power, debt-equity, return on equity, interest on working capital, capacity and energy charges including supplementary energy charges, recovery of tariff and incentives, operational norms for thermal and hydro stations, tariff determination for pumped hydro storage, compensation for part-load operation, sharing of gains from better-than-norm performance, refinancing and non-tariff income, and late payment surcharge. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: Tariff framework, applications and in-principle approval for conventional generators
True-up methodology for FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27
Capital cost, IDC/IEDC, sale of infirm power, debt-equity, RoE
Capacity charges and energy charges, including supplementary energy charges
Operational norms for thermal and hydro stations; compensation for part-load operation
Tariff determination for pumped hydro storage plants
Sharing of gains from operational norms, loan refinancing and non-tariff income

title: Draft TNERC (Terms and Conditions for Determination of Tariff from Non-Conventional Energy Generation Sources) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes new regulations for tariffs from non-conventional (renewable) energy sources. The draft makes competitive bidding the route for procuring power from grid-connected renewable projects, while providing for generic and project-specific tariffs, and sets financial principles (capital cost, debt-equity, loan tenure, depreciation, return on equity, working capital, O&M, rebate and late payment surcharge, sharing of carbon credits). It then sets technology-specific parameters for solar (including module degradation), wind (including repowering, refurbishment and life extension), biomass, small hydro, waste-to-energy and battery energy storage. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: Competitive bidding for procurement from grid-connected renewable projects
Generic and project-specific tariffs; petition process
Financial norms: capital cost, debt-equity, depreciation, RoE, O&M, working capital
Sharing of carbon credit and environmental attribute benefits
Technology parameters for solar, wind (including repowering), biomass, small hydro, waste-to-energy
Tariff determination for battery energy storage

title: Draft TNERC (Terms and Conditions for Determination of Tariff for Intra-State Transmission System) Regulations, 2026
summary: TNERC proposes new tariff regulations for the intra-State transmission system under a multi-year tariff framework. The draft sets out the MYT petition process and the true-up methodology for FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27, components of the transmission licensee's ARR (capital investment plan, capital base and asset register, return on equity, interest, depreciation, O&M and other costs), treatment of projects won through tariff-based competitive bidding, determination of Total Transmission Capacity, sharing of transmission charges with special provisions for open access customers, cost pools, exemptions and waivers, billing and recovery, and operational norms. This is a proposal; TNERC has extended the last date for comments on this and eight other draft regulations to 16 November 2026.
proposes: MYT framework and petitions for transmission licensees; true-up of FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27
ARR components: capital investment plan, capital base, RoE, interest, depreciation, O&M
Treatment of TBCB transmission projects under the MYT framework
Determination and revision of Total Transmission Capacity
Sharing of transmission charges, special provisions for open access customers, cost pools
Exemptions, waivers and rebates; billing and recovery; operational norms

title: Draft KERC Procurement of Energy from Renewable Sources Regulations, 2026.
summary: KERC proposes new regulations on renewable purchase obligations to replace its 2011 regulations, aligning Karnataka with the Government of India's revised Renewable Consumption Obligation notification of 27.09.2025. Distribution licensees, open access consumers above 1 MW and captive users with plants of 1 MW and above would have to meet a total RPO rising from 35.95% in 2026-27 to 43.33% in 2029-30, split into wind, hydro, distributed RE and other RE components. Obligations could be met through renewable power, RECs or the CERC buyout price, with SLDC monitoring compliance and possible action under Section 142. Tariffs for wind, solar MW-scale, mini-hydel, co-generation and biomass would be discovered through bidding. KERC's website lists 11.11.2026 as the last date for suggestions; the gazette notice of 22.10.2026 allows 30 days from publication. This is a proposal.
proposes: Components: wind RE, hydro RE (projects after 31.03.2024), distributed RE (under 10 MW) and other RE
Obligated: discoms, open access consumers above 1 MW and captive users with plants of 1 MW and above
Compliance through RE purchase, RECs or the CERC buyout price; open access and captive users may meet the total from any RE source
SLDC to monitor and report by 31 August each year; non-compliance may lead to Section 142 proceedings
Tariffs for wind, solar MW-scale, mini-hydel, co-generation and biomass through Section 63 bidding
REC-route generators to sell to ESCOMs at the lower of pooled power purchase cost or 75% of generic tariff
amends: Replaces KERC (Power Procurement from Renewable Sources by Distribution Licensee) Regulations, 2011

impact.headline: Open access above 1 MW or a captive plant in Karnataka? Check whether the proposed renewable obligation would cover you.
checks: Is your contract demand 1 MW or more, and do you draw more than 1 MW through open access?
Do you have a grid-connected captive plant of 1 MW or more, and on what fuel?
What share of your consumption is already renewable, and from which sources?
Do you have several sites in Karnataka under one legal entity?
impact.market_note: If adopted, Karnataka's RPO rises from 35.95% of consumption in 2026-27 to 43.33% in 2029-30. It binds open access consumers above 1 MW and captive users with plants of 1 MW and above, not only ESCOMs. ESCOMs face separate wind, hydro and distributed-RE sub-targets; OA and captive users can meet the total from any RE.

key_points.text: Total RPO: 35.95% (2026-27), 38.81%, 41.36%, 43.33% (2029-30); distributed RE rises from 2.70% to 4.50% and wind from 1.97% to 3.48%
Obligated: ESCOMs, OA consumers with contract demand of 1 MW and above drawing over 1 MW through OA, and captive users with grid-connected plants of 1 MW and above
Wind and hydro components count only from projects commissioned after 31.03.2024; distributed RE only from projects under 10 MW, and its shortfall cannot be covered by other RE
Compliance routes: RE from captive or any source (including traders, the market or storage), RECs including VPPA-linked RECs, or the CERC buyout price
Non-compliance or not furnishing data can lead to Section 142 proceedings

procurement.text: ESCOMs to source wind and hydro from projects commissioned after 31.03.2024 and distributed RE from projects under 10 MW, to meet sub-targets
Mini-hydel, MW-scale solar, wind, co-generation and biomass tariffs through Section 63 bidding
Captive RE plants counted for compliance must be at least 250 kW
A legal entity with several sites in Karnataka complies on a combined basis
Obligated entities report consumption and RE by 31 July; SLDC files the compliance report by 31 August

discoms.comment: If adopted, ESCOMs must meet the rising total plus wind, hydro and distributed-RE sub-targets, and a distributed-RE shortfall cannot be offset. Their base excludes OA, captive and green-tariff sales.

ci_consumers.comment: If adopted, OA consumers with contract demand of 1 MW and above drawing over 1 MW via OA carry an RPO on their OA consumption, and may meet it from any RE, RECs or the buyout price.

captive.comment: If adopted, captive users with grid-connected plants of 1 MW and above are obligated on self-consumption net of auxiliary use, excluding waste-heat generation and 50% of fossil co-generation.

re_developers.comment: If adopted, sub-targets create demand reserved for wind and hydro commissioned after 31.03.2024 and for RE projects under 10 MW. Generators taking RECs must sell to ESCOMs at the lower of pooled cost or 75% of generic tariff.

storage.comment: If adopted, RE bought through an energy storage system counts towards RPO compliance.

transmission.comment: If adopted, SLDC as State Agency verifies compliance for all obligated entities, frames accreditation procedures within three months, and reports by 31 August.

traders.comment: If adopted, RE bought from traders or the market counts, and RECs (including VPPA-linked) remain a compliance route for all obligated entities.

open_questions: The notice allows 30 days from publication in the Gazette (22.10.2026); KERC's listing showed 11.11.2026. Confirm the date with KERC.
Designated consumers under the Energy Conservation Act report through BEE; how the two compliance tracks reconcile is not spelt out.

figures.note: A proposal, not in force. Steps as set out in the draft regulations.

captive.position: We support the exclusions for waste heat and by-product gas generation, which recognise how industrial captive plants operate. We ask the Commission to clarify the coverage of renewable captive plants and to remove limits that keep smaller captive renewable capacity from counting.

points.clause: Regulation 2(1)(i)(c): captive consumer with a grid-connected captive plant of 1 MW and above
points.comment: The definition covers any grid-connected captive plant of 1 MW and above. It does not say whether a consumer whose only captive plant is renewable is an obligated entity. [Add your captive capacity by fuel.]
points.suggestion: Clarify that the 1 MW threshold refers to fossil-fuel captive capacity.

points.clause: Regulation 3(2)(III) and 3(3): exclusions from consumption
points.comment: We support excluding waste heat recovery and by-product gas generation, and half of fossil co-generation.
points.suggestion: Add a short definition of 'co-generation plant' so the 50% exclusion is applied uniformly.

points.clause: Regulation 4(1)(a), proviso: captive RE plant not less than 250 kW
points.comment: A captive renewable plant below 250 kW does not count. Many industrial sites have several smaller rooftop systems that together exceed this size.
points.suggestion: Apply the 250 kW limit to the consumer's total captive RE capacity in the State, consistent with the combined compliance allowed by Regulation 4(2).

points.clause: Regulation 8(3): certificates for self-consumption not eligible for sale
points.comment: Certificates issued for self-consumption cannot be sold. The draft does not say whether they can be used against the same company's RPO at another unit.
points.suggestion: Confirm that self-retained certificates can be redeemed against the RPO of any unit of the same legal entity in the State.

points.clause: Regulation 5(2) and 5(4): information and Section 142
points.comment: Captive users must furnish bills and other details 'in a time bound manner', with Section 142 exposure for delay.
points.suggestion: Fix the documents and date in the Regulations and provide a notice period before proceedings.

captive.closing: We request the Commission to consider these comments and to grant us an opportunity to be heard before the Regulations are finalised.

ci_consumers.position: We accept a renewable purchase obligation on large open access consumers and support the freedom to meet it from any renewable source. We ask for clarity on who is covered and how consumption is counted, and for a fair process before any penal proceedings.

points.clause: Regulation 2(1)(i): definition of obligated entity
points.comment: An open access consumer is obligated if it has contracted demand of 1 MW and above and avails more than 1 MW through open access. It is unclear whether several connections of one company are added together to reach the threshold. [Add your contract demand and open access quantum.]
points.suggestion: State that the threshold applies to each connection, and that Regulation 4(2) only combines units that are each obligated.

points.clause: Regulation 3(2)(II): consumption on which RPO is computed
points.comment: RPO applies to energy availed through open access from all sources, excluding supply from the licensee. A consumer buying only renewable power through open access would already exceed the target.
points.suggestion: Confirm that renewable energy bought through open access counts in full, and that a surplus can be carried forward or converted to certificates.

points.clause: Regulation 3(5), proviso: open access and captive users may meet total RPO from any RE
points.comment: We support this. Component-wise targets would not be workable for a single consumer.
points.suggestion: Retain as drafted.

points.clause: Regulation 4(1)(b) and (c): certificates and buyout price
points.comment: Compliance through RECs, including under virtual PPAs, and the buyout price are welcome options.
points.suggestion: Confirm that RECs from a virtual PPA with a project outside Karnataka qualify, and publish the applicable buyout price before each year begins.

points.clause: Regulation 5(2) and 5(4): reporting by 31 July and Section 142
points.comment: Consumers must report by 31 July and a delay or shortfall can lead straight to Section 142 proceedings on the State Agency's report.
points.suggestion: Provide a notice and a thirty-day period to cure before the State Agency recommends action.

ci_consumers.closing: We request the Commission to consider these comments and to grant us an opportunity to be heard before the Regulations are finalised.

discoms.position: We support aligning the State's RPO framework with the Government of India's notification and a single compliance track. Our comments are on the pace of the trajectory, the distributed RE component that a licensee cannot control, and the data duties placed on licensees.

points.clause: Regulation 3(4): RPO trajectory
points.comment: Total RPO rises from 35.95% in 2026-27 to 43.33% in 2029-30. The draft does not set out the cost of meeting it or how it fits approved power procurement plans. [Add your present RE share and tied-up capacity.]
points.suggestion: Publish the cost and capacity assessment behind the trajectory, and allow a shortfall of up to [10%] of the target to be carried forward by one year.

points.clause: Regulation 3(5)(c) and (e): distributed RE component
points.comment: The distributed RE share rises from 2.70% to 4.50% and its shortfall cannot be met from any other source. Rooftop and small-scale additions depend on consumers' decisions, not the licensee's.
points.suggestion: Allow a distributed RE shortfall to be met from other RE for the first two years, or to be carried forward.

points.clause: Regulation 3(5)(a) and (b): wind and hydro only from projects commissioned after 31.03.2024
points.comment: We support the flexibility in clause (e) to meet a wind or hydro shortfall from surplus in other RE, as new hydro capacity is limited.
points.suggestion: Retain clause (e) as drafted.

points.clause: Regulation 5(2), first proviso: licensees to furnish consumption of open access and captive users
points.comment: Licensees must supply consumption and meter data of every open access and captive user 'in a time bound manner' without a format or date, and non-furnishing can lead to Section 142 proceedings.
points.suggestion: Specify the format and a date in the Regulations, and provide that data is filed once on the State Agency's portal.

discoms.closing: We request the Commission to consider these comments and to grant us an opportunity to be heard before the Regulations are finalised.

re_developers.position: We welcome the higher trajectory and the separate wind, hydro and distributed RE components, which give investors a clear signal. Our comments are on the terms for projects that choose the certificate route and on tariff discovery for small projects.

points.clause: Regulation 3(5)(a) and (b): wind and hydro components from projects commissioned after 31.03.2024
points.comment: We support the vintage condition. It directs new demand to new capacity.
points.suggestion: Retain as drafted.

points.clause: Regulation 8(2), second proviso (c): sale to ESCOMs at the lower of pooled cost or 75% of generic tariff
points.comment: A generator opting for certificates must sell its electricity to ESCOMs at the lower of the pooled cost of power purchase or 75% of the generic tariff. This is below the pooled cost benchmark and removes the choice of buyer. [Add your project's expected realisation.]
points.suggestion: Fix the price at the pooled cost of power purchase and allow sale to any buyer, as the certificate already separates the green attribute.

points.clause: Regulation 8(2), second proviso (b): one-year bar after premature termination of a PPA
points.comment: A project whose PPA ends early is barred from the certificate scheme for a year, whatever the reason for termination.
points.suggestion: Exempt projects whose PPA is terminated for the buyer's default.

points.clause: Regulation 9(2): tariff through bidding for mini-hydel, wind, co-generation and biomass
points.comment: Tariffs for these sources are to be discovered only through Section 63 bidding. Projects below 10 MW, which the distributed RE component relies on, cannot absorb bidding costs and timelines.
points.suggestion: Continue generic tariffs for projects below 10 MW.

re_developers.closing: We request the Commission to consider these comments and to grant us an opportunity to be heard before the Regulations are finalised.

title: Draft Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Indian Electricity Grid Code) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026
summary: CERC proposes a broad second amendment to the Indian Electricity Grid Code. It would introduce a congestion charge on regional entities whose deviations push flows on inter- or intra-regional links beyond Total Transfer Capability, payable on top of deviation charges at a rate CERC sets by order. It sets rules for scheduling infirm power after a successful trial run, offering it first to contracted buyers with seven days' notice. It brings pumped storage plants and energy storage systems more fully into scheduling, despatch and ancillary service provisions, revises the timelines and treatment for units under reserve shutdown, and shortens the gap between schedule revisions in two phases, the second from 1 April 2027. Comments closed on 2 November 2026 and the public hearing was held on 4 November 2026; the final amendment is awaited.
proposes: New Regulation 30A: congestion charge on regional entities causing flows beyond TTC, in addition to deviation charges
New Regulation 25A: infirm power scheduled only after a successful trial run, offered first to contracted buyers with 7 days' notice
Pumped storage plants and ESS brought into scheduling, despatch and reserve provisions
Reserve shutdown: new D-1 timelines (1430/1530/1600/1800 hrs) and rules for on-bar and off-bar declared capacity
NLDC may run SCUC at any time of day to commit or decommit units for grid security
Shorter revision timelines in two phases, the second from 01.04.2027
New definitions including congestion charge, default trigger date (75 days after RPC accounts) and REIA

related.label: Public Hearing will be held on 04.11.2026 at 10:30 AM.

title: Draft GERC (Electricity Supply Code and Related Matters) (Fifth Amendment) Regulations, 2026
summary: GERC proposes a wide update of Gujarat's Electricity Supply Code. All new connections would get smart meters with prepayment functionality or prepayment meters, unless the Commission allows an exception. LT connections up to 150 kW could be released on the applicant's declaration, with the test report filed online within 45 days, following a state government order of July 2026. Applicants doing their own extension work would pay only supervision charges, but would face demand and minimum charges if they do not finish within the standard time and a further 60 days after notice. Bills above Rs 10,000 would have to be paid electronically, with a small rebate for prompt e-payment. Temporary connections for construction could run up to three years, and safety references move to the CEA's 2023 regulations. This is a proposal; GERC's listing gives no last date for comments, so check the public notice.
proposes: Smart prepaid or prepayment meters for all new connections, subject to exemption by the Commission
LT connections up to 150 kW released on declaration; test report online within 45 days
Self-executed extension work: supervision charges only; charges apply if not completed within standard time plus 60 days after notice
Mandatory e-payment for bills above Rs 10,000; rebate of 0.01% or Rs 50 (whichever is less) for timely e-payment
Temporary connections up to 12 months, or up to 3 years for construction
Smart meters read remotely at least monthly; consumption data via website, app or SMS
Notices may be served by registered e-mail
Safety, wiring and protection requirements aligned with CEA safety regulations, 2023
amends: GERC (Electricity Supply Code and Related Matters) Regulations, 2015

title: Draft GERC (Standards of Performance of Distribution Licensees) (First Amendment) Regulations, 2026
summary: GERC proposes tighter standards for Gujarat's distribution licensees. New connections, load enhancements, shifting and conversion of service that need no network work would have to be energised within 3 days in metropolitan areas, 7 days in other urban areas and 10 days in rural areas, with automatic compensation of Rs 50 a day for delay. Longer timelines would apply where the network has to be extended, from 15 days for an LT line up to 150 metres to 180 days for EHT lines or sub-stations. Reliability would be measured under IEEE Standard 1366-2022, adding a new index (CAIFI) reported quarterly and annually, and safety and earthing would follow the CEA's 2023 safety regulations. This is a proposal; GERC's listing gives no last date for comments, so check the public notice.
proposes: Connection time limits without network work: 3 days (metropolitan), 7 days (other urban), 10 days (rural)
Network extensions: 15 days (LT up to 150 m) up to 180 days (EHT line or sub-station)
Automatic compensation of Rs 50 per day of delay in energisation
Licensee must tell applicants the expected energisation date
Reliability indices under IEEE 1366-2022, adding CAIFI, reported quarterly and annually
Construction, maintenance and earthing testing under CEA safety regulations, 2023
amends: GERC (Standards of Performance of Distribution Licensees) Regulations, 2023
